author: iceberg-ua
body:
Every user-facing string was hardcoded C#, so this builds the localization layer from scratch: flat dot-notation keys in one JSON file per language, looked up through ILocalizationService.

The lookup logic lives in Core rather than in the MAUI project. Only two things genuinely need MAUI - reading a packaged asset and writing a preference - so those became interfaces with MAUI implementations in the host. Keeping the rest in Core is what makes it testable at all: the net10.0 test project cannot reference a net10.0-android project.

A key missing from the active language falls back to English; one missing from English too renders as [[key]], so a forgotten translation is visible during testing instead of blank. Translations load before the first window exists, so nothing paints in the wrong language first.

Position abbreviations stay untranslated. GK/DEF/MID/FWD read the same in all three languages and have to fit a badge a few characters wide.

Team names are rebuilt in the UI from the team's index rather than shown from Team.Name, which Core generates as "Team A" with no localization of its own - otherwise the Teams screen kept an English label.

author: mradfo21
body: ## What & why Instrumented play-testing showed the "flashing / never-settles / black" feel comes from the realtime auto-advance being **faster than the world model can render**. In realtime autoplay, once the video showed, the game advanced — hard-resetting the seed-locked LingBot world — after only **7s** (`AUTOPLAY_REALTIME_WATCH_MS`). Measured with Playwright, LingBot takes **~14s just to START streaming** after a re-anchor and needs several more seconds to visibly evolve. So the 7s window reset the world before it ever settled, and the player never actually got to see the live world. ## Change - `AUTOPLAY_REALTIME_WATCH_MS`: `7000` → `22000` (let the live world play/evolve before advancing) - `AUTOPLAY_REALTIME_MAX_WAIT_MS`: `20000` → `30000` (don't force-advance while a slow world is still appearing) Only affects realtime auto-play pacing. Manual play (player-driven choices) is unchanged, and the `window.__AUTOPLAY_WATCH_MS__` override used by the e2e test is preserved. ## Testing - `node --check static/js/standalone.js` passes. - e2e override mechanism (`__AUTOPLAY_WATCH_MS__`) intact.

author: megaredhand
body:
## Problem

`merkleize()` padded the leaf layer out to `next_power_of_two(chunks.len())` with `ZERO_HASHES[0]`, then hashed that layer as if it held data:

```rust
layer.resize(real_leaf_count, ZERO_HASHES[0]);        // materializes the padding
for zero_hash in ZERO_HASHES.iter().take(real_depth) {
    let mut next = Vec::with_capacity(layer.len() / 2);
    for pair in layer.chunks(2) { next.push(hash_nodes(hasher, ..)) }  // hashes zero subtrees
    layer = next;
}
```

The precomputed zero hashes were only applied *above* `real_depth`, collapsing the virtual levels between `next_power_of_two(chunks.len())` and the type's `limit`. Empty subtrees *inside* the padded real region had been turned into ordinary leaves by the `resize`, so they got hashed.

Cost was `next_power_of_two(N) - 1` hashes, which **doubles when N crosses a power of two**:

| N | `real_leaf_count` | hashes |
|---|---|---|
| 65 536 | 65 536 | 65 535 |
| **65 537** | **131 072** | **131 071** |

For a beacon chain `SszList<H256, 2^18>` (H256 is exactly one chunk, so `chunks.len()` equals the list length) that step lands precisely at slot 2^16, where roughly half the hashing covers subtrees that are provably all zeros. The waste then decays as N approaches the next power of two.

## Fix

Fold only the real chunks. When a level ends on an odd node, the missing right sibling roots an all-zero subtree, so substitute `ZERO_HASHES[level]` instead of hashing what is under it:

```rust
let mut layer: Vec<Node> = chunks.to_vec();
let mut next: Vec<Node> = Vec::with_capacity(layer.len().div_ceil(2));

for zero_hash in ZERO_HASHES.iter().take(real_depth) {
    next.clear();                                  // reuses capacity, never reallocates
    let mut pairs = layer.chunks_exact(2);
    for pair in &mut pairs {
        next.push(hash_nodes(hasher, &pair[0], &pair[1]));
    }
    if let [odd] = pairs.remainder() {             // frontier: right sibling is all zeros
        next.push(hash_nodes(hasher, odd, zero_hash));
    }
    core::mem::swap(&mut layer, &mut next);
}
```

Cost becomes `O(N)` plus one hash per virtual level. **Roots are unchanged.**

Two secondary wins fell out:

- The two buffers are allocated once and swapped per level, so folding no longer allocates per level (previously one `Vec` per level, ~2N nodes over the run). Peak memory is ~1.5N nodes, same as before.
- Empty `chunks` with a `limit` now returns `ZERO_HASHES[depth]` directly instead of hashing `depth` levels of zeros.

## Hash counts

Exact, measured with a counting hasher, `limit = 2^18`:

| N | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 65 536 | 65 537 | 65 537 | unchanged |
| **65 537** | **131 072** | **65 553** | **2.00x** |
| 100 000 | 131 072 | 100 007 | 1.31x |
| 131 073 | 262 143 | 131 089 | 2.00x |

## Benchmarks

Criterion, identical settings on both sides, `--baseline` captured from this branch with only `crates/ssz-merkle/src/lib.rs` stashed, so the new bench cases exist in both runs.

| Case | Chunk count | Change |
|---|---|---|
| `merkleize_with_limit/65537_of_262144` | 65 537 | **−50.1%** |
| `hash_tree_root/beacon_state/300000` | 300 000 | **−13.1%** (CI −15.2 to −11.2) |
| `hash_tree_root/beacon_state/100000` | 100 000 | **−13.9%** (CI −21.2 to −6.4) |
| `hash_tree_root/list_validator/10000` | 10 000 | −7.8% |
| `hash_tree_root/list_validator/1000` | 1 000 | −3.6% |
| `merkleize_with_limit/65536_of_262144` | 65 536 | no change (p=0.59) |
| `merkleize_with_limit/1024_of_1048576` | 1 024 | no change (p=0.71) |
| `merkleize_with_limit/256_of_4096` | 256 | no change (p=0.56) |
| `merkleize_with_limit/64_of_1024` | 64 | no change (p=0.52) |
| `hash_tree_root/beacon_state/16384` | 16 384 | no change (p=0.35) |

The −50.1% matches the predicted 2.00x hash-count reduction. Every power-of-two case is flat, which is the correct signature: those have no zero subtrees to skip.

Caveat on method: measured on a laptop, and the wide CI on `beacon_state/100000` (10 samples of a ~280 ms benchmark) reflects that. The `merkleize` group at 100 samples is the tighter measurement and the one that isolates the change.

### Why the suite missed this

Every pre-existing `merkleize` benchmark used a power-of-two chunk count (`1, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024, 4096`, and `64/1024`, `256/4096`, `1024/2^20` for the limit cases), where `next_power_of_two(N) == N` and the waste is exactly zero. The bug was invisible by construction. This adds the `65_536`/`65_537` pair, which straddles the boundary.

### One regression caught during review

An earlier in-place variant of the fold used explicit indices, costing three bounds checks per node. That regressed `256_of_4096` by +1.2% and `1024_of_1048576` by +2.2% while still delivering the 2x win. Keeping reads on a `chunks_exact` iterator restores the original codegen; all power-of-two cases now report no change.

## Tests

Three tests added:

- `merkleize_matches_fully_materialized_oracle` — compares against a naive reference that materializes every leaf including the zero ones, over N = 0..70 × 6 limits. Pins the roots.
- `merkleize_does_not_hash_zero_subtrees` — a counting hasher pins the **exact** hash count against a closed-form expectation, so the cost cannot regress silently.
- `merkleize_cost_is_linear_across_power_of_two_boundary` — the direct regression guard. Fails on `main` with `one extra chunk added 1023 hashes (1024 -> 1031, 1025 -> 2054)`.

Plus `merkleize_empty_with_limit_is_the_precomputed_zero_hash` for the new empty-chunks shortcut.

Verification:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Full workspace suite, `--all-features` | 1177 passed, 0 failed |
| Consensus-spec vectors v1.6.1 (general + mainnet + minimal) | 891 pass, roots identical |
| New cost tests, run against `main` | fail as expected |
| `cargo fmt --check`, clippy, `no_std` + `alloc` build | clean |

`cargo check -p libssz-merkle --no-default-features` (without `alloc`) fails, but that is pre-existing and inside `libssz`, not this crate; confirmed against a stashed tree.

## Follow-ups, not in this PR

- `bench_merkleize` (the `limit=None` group) still uses only power-of-two counts, so it would not catch a regression here either.
- The iai-callgrind targets would give noise-free instruction counts for a 65 537 case.
- `merkleize_progressive` inherits the fix through its partial subtrees and may be worth re-measuring.

author: harkiratmangat
body:
## What this is

Two things that ended up entangled, so they ship together: the **Dior's Builds → Dioreo** rename, and the mobile-polish round that was in flight when it landed.

Full account in [`docs/CHANGELOG.md`](docs/CHANGELOG.md) under v2.52.0. The short version:

## The rename

Documented the way a product rename has to be, not by find-and-replace alone.

- **LICENSE → Dioreo Source-Available License v1.1** (`LicenseRef-Dioreo-Source-Available-1.1`), with a new **§18**: change of name only, no assignment or change of ownership, references to the former name still bind, copies held under v1.0 remain valid, old SPDX id still denotes v1.0. **§1.5 now covers both names** — retiring a name does not release it.
- **Terms 1.5** and **Privacy 1.8**, each with a name-change clause and a revision row. Privacy states explicitly that **the controller did not change**: no new controller, processor, recipient or purpose, and Appendix A is untouched.
- Terms' revision history also records that **1.2 and 1.3 were never published** — the header jumped 1.1 → 1.4 on 1 August while the row describing it was written as "1.2". Recorded honestly rather than quietly renumbered.

**Deliberately NOT renamed**, because the boundary matters more than the consistency: the three record files and `docs/archive/` (history says what it was called at the time), the dated specs, the VM / systemd / dev-DB identifiers, and **the repo folder** — the memory-store slug derives from that path. `CLAUDE.md` records the whole boundary.

## The mobile round

- Landing page introduces the bot instead of the paperwork; the legal set keeps its numbered list under its own label, and its "*N* documents" line stays **derived**.
- Code blocks rebuilt as a header strip + the code. The old overlay control needed three workarounds (opaque background, reserved right padding, a 3.6rem top pad on touch) and still read as a disc in an empty band. Copying now shows a **Copied** bubble.
- Legal footer rhythm now matches Contributing — 54px above the link row, 82px below the sign-off, against 96 and 28.
- Back-to-top on Contributing and Contributors. Its CSS and behaviour had been loading there for weeks with no button to drive.
- LICENSE and NOTICE offer their plain-text originals from the section index, reachable from anywhere on the page.
- Contributor plates fill the row instead of hugging the left edge.

## A real defect the rename exposed

The CLA slip's copy button carried a literal `Copy` text node between the CLA line and the paragraph after it, so the page read *"…in §5 of the LICENSE **copy** If you'd rather…"*. `verify()` had reported 100% for four days purely because it slices runs at a fixed stride from word one and no boundary landed on that seam. Removing one word upstream shifted every boundary and the next build caught it. **The defect never changed — only the arithmetic did.**

Two CSS specificity bugs were caught the same way, by reading computed values off the rendered page: a narrow-width `.doc` margin losing to the later `.doc` rule, and the contributor wall's column key losing to `.card p` — the latter had *no rule at all*.

## ⚠️ Ships with one known break, on purpose

Every GitHub URL now reads `github.com/HarkiratMangat/dioreo` and the repo is still `Diors-Builds`, so the Source button and the clone snippet 404 until `gh repo rename dioreo` is run. Filed `[P1 · XS]`. The alternative was landing the release with the old URLs and re-editing seven files afterwards; GitHub 301-redirects after a rename, so either order ends up correct and only this one has a window.

## Verification

- `npm run site` — 13/13 gates
- `npm test` — 18/18 hook self-tests
- `npm run docs:audit --diff main` — **37/37**, conservation check included
- Footer and code-block geometry measured off the rendered pages, not estimated

author: byebrianwong
body:
Asked *"what do I have due today?"*, Claude answered that nothing in DoDone had a due date set — "or any date, as far as I can tell" — while the Today screen was full. It was telling the truth about the wrong field.

The MCP surface was entirely `due_date`-shaped, and DoDone schedules on `when_date`.

## What was broken

- `create_task`/`update_task` had **no `when_date` parameter at all** — a client could not schedule a task through the MCP.
- `list_tasks` could only filter `due_before`/`due_after`, so "what's on today" had no query that could answer it.
- `get_focus_tasks` printed `(due: …)` and nothing else, so tasks scheduled for today rendered as bare titles.
- Nothing told the client today's date, and the hosted transport resolved it from a UTC process clock — a user behind UTC got tomorrow's answer for the last hours of their evening.

## What changed

- **`get_agenda`** — the date query: overdue first, then one section per day, covering both date fields.
- **Both fields on every path** — `when_date`/`when_time` added to create, update, and list filters; `when_before`/`when_after` added to `TaskFilterInput` and `TasksApi.list`.
- **No date emitted bare** — every task carries `{when_relative, due_relative, overdue, summary}` resolved against the user's real today: `"scheduled for 2026-08-03 (Monday, today)"`, not `"2026-08-03"`.
- **Timezone-correct today** via `user_preferences.timezone` (`src/clock.ts`), plus `TasksApi.getDatedBetween`/`getOverdue`, which take the day as a parameter rather than reading the clock. The timezone is cached per instance; the day is recomputed per call, since the stdio process sits through midnight.
- **`SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS`** states the two-field model at initialization, and each date-touching tool description repeats it — a client that has already picked its tool has stopped reading descriptions, and one that reads only descriptions never sees the instructions.

## Verification

`pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm test` pass (27 new tests in `dates.test.ts` covering DST spans, month/year boundaries, overdue bucketing, and agenda rendering).

Exercised read-only against live data through an in-memory MCP client. The same question that produced *"nothing has a due date"*:

```
Today is 2026-08-03 (Monday, today) in America/Los_Angeles.

## 2026-08-03 · Monday · today
- [p1] Clean up room — scheduled
- [p1] Figure out healthypaws pet insurance — scheduled
- [p2] Renew progressive auto insurance — scheduled
…8 tasks
## 2026-08-06 · Thursday · in 3 days
- [p4] Fix screen door — scheduled
```

## Follow-up

A separate PR will rename these fields for good: `when_date` → `scheduled_date`, `due_date` → `deadline_date`, everywhere including the Postgres columns, retiring the word "due" from user- and agent-facing text. This PR keeps the current names and fixes the semantics.

Note: the local stdio server serves the old behaviour until `apps/mcp` is rebuilt and Claude Code restarted; the hosted connector until the web app redeploys.

author: jd
body:
Two things in the capture skill helped a stale, identity-carrying screenshot
live in the docs for two years.

- **The documented image root was wrong.** It said
  `src/content/docs/images/`; the real one is `src/content/images/` — every
  page imports `../../images/...` and the collection reads nothing under
  `docs/images/`. Anyone following the skill wrote to a directory the site does
  not serve. It was flagged as a follow-up a fortnight ago and never fixed.
- **Neither capture path said anything about account identity, and this repo
  is public.** Shots taken from a live logged-in session have already published
  real org, user and repository names. The skill now says to prefer a capture
  that carries no account identity, and to crop the sidebar out when a live
  session is unavoidable.

The sidebar rule is the durable half: it carries the org name, the signed-in
user's name and their avatar, and it is also the fastest-changing part of the
dashboard, so a shot framed around it goes stale every time a nav item is
renamed even when the documented feature has not moved.

Also drops the internal repository name from both files. This repo is public
and that repository is not, so naming it disclosed something the instructions
never needed — the tool is described by what it does instead.

Refs MRGFY-8272

author: yvesas
body:
**Console phases 4 and 5** — the last two it had. Stacked conceptually on #69 (playground) but touching different files; both are on `main`.

## Config

An editor over `config/*.json`. The rule it rests on, from doc 21 §5:

> **The console edits files. It does not replace files with a database.**

A table would cost the Git history, the code review of a price change, the fork model and a reproducible deploy — and would buy a form.

- **Validated with the harness's own parsers** — `parseModelConfig`, `parsePersona` — not a second schema that agrees today and drifts by Christmas. Nothing that would stop the harness starting reaches the disk. *(Writing an invalid fixture is how the test suite came to demonstrate that a `sensitive` route may not use a cheap model.)*
- **Secrets are never resolved.** `connectors.json` keeps `${VAR}` exactly as written: resolving to display puts a client secret on a web page, resolving to save writes it into Git. It is checked as a *shape* rather than through the harness's loader, which reads the environment — a secret unset on this machine is not a reason to refuse somebody's edit.
- **Three files, by name.** A path from a form is input; without the allow-list, `../../.env` is readable and the console is a secret viewer.
- **`config/` is mounted read-write** in compose. An editor whose changes vanish on the next rebuild discards your work.

## Evals

The framework existed and was reachable only from a script — enough for CI, not enough for the loop the console is for: change a route, run the cases, see whether the cheap tier still gets them right.

**Confidence is shown beside each failure**, because wrong-and-sure and wrong-and-unsure need different fixes: the first is a module description that misleads the router, the second is a genuinely ambiguous case.

## Three boundaries the build drew, not the design

**A client component importing `config-files.ts` dragged `pg` — and therefore `net` and `dns` — toward the browser.** What both sides need now lives in a module with no harness import.

**TypeScript rewrites `.js`→`.ts`; Turbopack does not.** One file cannot satisfy both toolchains, so the console keeps its extensionless imports and its test moved to `console/tests/`, beside the code it exercises, where vitest picks it up regardless.

**A webpack config to bridge them made the *container* build fail while the local one passed** — and `docker compose up` then served the previous image without a word. Worth knowing: `docker compose up -d --build` will not tell you the build failed. It is why the nav in this PR is verified by reading the compiled chunk inside the container, not by trusting the page.

**15 new tests (819 total).** Verified in the container: all eight pages render, and the editor reads the mounted `config/` from the host.

author: lodar
body:
## DIVE-2716 — a tier HOLD is a verdict on a TASK; it was being spent on the AGENT

**Measured 2026-08-04 19:35Z:** 4 agents holding, 122 rows queued, nothing claimed in 2h35m. `main`'s queue had been blocked since 2026-07-30 — five days.

### The defect

The wake loop picked ONE todo per agent (`_hb_pick_task`, `LIMIT 1`). When DIVE-1065's tier guard refused to auto-drive that row, it ran `continue` — on the **agent's** iteration, not the row's. Selection is deterministic, so the next tick picked the same row, held it again, and skipped the agent again. Five held rows head-of-line blocked 122 runnable ones.

The falsified premise is in the guard's own comment: *"a hold skips ONE agent's wake this tick and never aborts the tick."* Both halves are true **per tick**. Per-event isolation says nothing about an event that repeats with identical input, and this one repeated every five minutes.

### The fix

**The guard is unchanged.** Its verdict is now scoped to the task it was made about: `_hb_pick_tasks` returns candidates in the same DIVE-979 priority/critical-path order and the loop takes the first one the guard clears. A held row stays held, is never the wake target, and still names itself in the log. The scan is bounded (`_HB_PICK_SCAN=25`) and hitting the bound is logged as "rows past the cap were NOT examined" rather than reported as an idle agent.

### Evidence

All measured on `e690271` (parent `12c7ac2`), each mutation confirmed landed by diff before running.

**The harness reds on the pre-fix tree.** Run whole against `origin/main`'s `cmd_heartbeat.sh`: `rc=1`, 14 arms red. An anchor that passes pre-fix would be testing the wrong thing.

**The anchor reproduces the stall, not a proxy for it.** Held head + 5 runnable rows behind it, same assignee: pre-fix reaches **zero** of the 5, post-fix reaches exactly 1. Graded for vacuity — the pre-fix tick must still log the hold, or "no wake" would be attributable to a dead harness. The fixture is self-seeded in a scratch sqlite db and reads **no live board**, so the parked blocking heads cannot satisfy it by accident.

**Guard and scheduler are separable.** Mutating each half alone:

| mutation | arms red only here |
|---|---|
| guard verdict neutered | **7** (e.g. "a fully-held queue wakes NOBODY", "held urgent row stays todo") |
| scheduler revert | **2** ("a queue holding runnable work never leaves the agent idle", "ANCHOR/N: post-fix reaches one of the rows the pre-fix tick could not") |

The scheduler revert was run two ways — `continue`→`break`, and `_HB_PICK_SCAN=1` (which *is* the old `LIMIT 1`) — and both agree.

Worth stating plainly: an assertion of the form *"the tick wakes row X"* reds under **both** defects, because neutering the guard makes the tick wake the held row instead. Arms shaped that way cannot say which half broke. The two scheduler-only arms deliberately name no row.

**The skip is observable, not just logged.** `tierHeld` was being emitted in the tick summary but **graded by nothing** — the harness sent that stdout to `/dev/null`. It is now asserted, with `MISSING` distinguished from `0`: a held board asserts `>= 1`, an unheld board asserts exactly `0`, so a constant cannot pass. This matters because stepping over a held head removes the blocking symptom that made this bug findable at all: DIVE-2459 sat held from 2026-07-30 and went unnoticed for five days. An unobservable skip would trade a loud permanent stall for a quiet permanent hold.

### Tests

`tests/heartbeat_tier_head_of_line_unit.sh` — new, 32 arms, 7.4s, drives the real `cmd_heartbeat_tick`.
`tests/heartbeat_tier_guard_unmeasured_unit.sh` — the guard block moved inside a candidate loop, so its verbatim extraction now ends at an explicit sentinel; it still accepts the old terminator so the pinned pre-fix copy extracts exactly as before.

Core tier: **235/235 harnesses passed, 0 failures.** The run exits 4 on wall-clock budget (438s local vs 300s), which is a contended-VM reading — this box measures ~45% high and CI last measured 270s/300s pristine at 233 harnesses. Deliberately **not** demoting on a local number; the CI budget line governs.

### Deploy note

This host runs `/usr/local/bin/5dive`, self-updated daily from the newest **release tag** — merging does not deploy it. The four parked blocking heads must stay parked until the installed binary actually carries this change, or they return to the head of four real queues in front of a pre-fix scheduler.

author: sondrateconsulting-ryan
body:
## The bug

In the field-observed exhausted-window response (2026-08-04; the spelling is undocumented), GitHub answered **HTTP 200** with an `errors` entry `{type: "RATE_LIMIT", message: "API rate limit already exceeded for user ID <id>"}` (`<id>` redacted) and header `x-ratelimit-remaining: 0`. That type spelling (no "ED") is distinct from the documented mid-window spelling `RATE_LIMITED`. `classifyGraphql` (scripts/github.ts) matched only `RATE_LIMITED`, so the already-exceeded shape fell through to the 2xx-with-body-errors branch and classified **fatal**. Consequences:

- `graphql()` armed **no bucket pause** (fatal returns `pauseUntilMs: null`) and threw `GithubApiError` instead of `ThrottleExhausted`
- `discoverBranchHeads` recorded a **permanent** discovery-failure errors row instead of taking the transient requeue-throttle path
- With no bucket pause, each active owner worker could continue to its next repo while the window remained exhausted, producing one bogus permanent error row per affected repo

Observed field error string:

```
branch discovery failed: graphql: RATE_LIMIT: API rate limit already exceeded for user ID <id>
```

(In the observed run, the TUI showed remaining=0 — its rate-limit panel is fed from raw response headers, independent of classification.)

## The fix

One production line: the `classifyGraphql` rate-limit predicate now matches **both exact type literals** — `RATE_LIMITED` and `RATE_LIMIT`. Exact literals only, no regex and no message matching (reviewer-confirmed: the rate-limited branch runs before the 403 permission handling, so message matching could reclassify a permission error that merely quotes the phrase). SSO precedence stays ahead of the check. The existing remaining-based logic then does the right thing: remaining `"0"` → primary (a valid `x-ratelimit-reset` becomes reset epoch + skew with the existing floor/cap; a missing or invalid reset uses the 60-second fallback; exhausting `MAX_ATTEMPTS` or the cumulative pause budget yields `ThrottleExhausted` → existing requeue path); nonzero remaining → secondary.

Plus four stale-comment updates in the same file naming both spellings (three in the original commit; the fourth — the SSO short-circuit block — landed in review remediation) and two PROMPT.md §4/§5.B spec-site updates recording the field-observed spelling (review remediation). **No** orchestrate.ts or TUI source changes and no new log/progress event kinds or tokens; the corrected shape now flows through the existing throttle/requeue telemetry.

## Test plan

Against the old classifier, the added tests produce four failing tests — fatal misclassification in the unit fixtures and `GithubApiError: graphql: RATE_LIMIT: slow down` from the wiring tests; with the one-line fix they pass.

- [x] unit: `RATE_LIMIT` + remaining `"0"` + reset → **primary** with exact `untilMs` (reset×1000 + 5000) — mirror of the `RATE_LIMITED` fixture
- [x] unit: `RATE_LIMIT` + nonzero remaining → **secondary**
- [x] unit (pin): SSO parity — 403 + `x-github-sso` + `RATE_LIMIT` body stays **fatal with ssoRequired**, twin of the `RATE_LIMITED` pin. This pins SSO-over-throttle precedence and is not a blanket assertion that a rate-limit body is never fatal
- [x] unit (named regression pin): the observed field shape — status 200, remaining `"0"`, `[{type:"RATE_LIMIT", message:"API rate limit already exceeded for user ID 123"}]` → **primary**
- [x] wiring: the two **existing** graphql() tests parameterized over both spellings — "far-future reset sleeps exactly MAX_PAUSE_MS, then retries" and "the graphql bucket has its own cumulative pause budget" (ThrottleExhausted, budget persists)
- [x] deliberately **no** orchestrate-level full-stack test: the suite's client uses a no-op `sleepImpl` with the real clock, so a funded pause would busy-wait until wall-clock reset; the ThrottleExhausted→throttled mapping is already covered by "processRepo branch-discovery throttle (§4, site c)" in orchestrate.test.ts
- [x] `bun test`: 2608 pass / 0 fail (includes the repo invariant scans)
- [x] `bun run typecheck`: clean
- [x] post-remediation (comment/doc-only commits): suite re-run 2608 pass / 0 fail, typecheck clean

## Review remediation (post-review commits)

A six-agent `/review-pr` pass (verdict: APPROVE — 0 Critical) with codex cross-validation of every finding produced four prose-only remediation commits; a three-reviewer santa loop (Opus 4.6 @ xhigh, GPT-5.5 @ xhigh, GPT-5.6 Sol @ ultra) returned unanimous first-round NICE on the remediation diff. Zero behavior change: the four remediation commits change only TypeScript comments and PROMPT.md; no executable TypeScript changed from `abbf31f`.

- `0dad797` — the SSO short-circuit comment was a fourth `RATE_LIMITED`-referencing block adjacent to the predicate; the original sweep updated the other three. Now names both spellings.
- `a508803` — PROMPT.md §4 and §5.B now record the field-observed already-exceeded `RATE_LIMIT` spelling at both GraphQL throttle sites; the §5.B parenthetical "GraphQL throttles arrive as HTTP 200" was overbroad against §4's own 200-or-403 secondary rule and now reads "can be body-signalled on HTTP 200".
- `5402be5` — the SSO/`RATE_LIMIT` pin's comment now states what the pin guards: SSO-over-throttle precedence when both signals coexist, not the type literal (the SSO short-circuit returns before `bodyErrors` is read; the classify fixtures pin the literal itself).
- `4e7c210` — local re-wrap of the exit-1-by-design comment (the original diff left a two-word orphan line).

## DISCLOSURE — frozen-bench reach

`benchGh.ts` imports the **production** `classifyGraphql` (benchGh.ts:15), so this change alters behavior reachable from the §8-frozen bench harness. Already-collected ADR-0001 evidence stands — it ran at its recorded digest. Any future gate-relevant bench collection requires a fresh §8 plan amendment plus one adversarial review round before data collection; changing the frozen surface restarts the whole matrix. The bench lane's own local `RATE_LIMITED` literals (benchGh.ts:430, benchT1.ts:219) are deliberately untouched here (bench-only, §8-frozen; separate amendment later).

## Follow-ups (deferred/cut — reviewer-ratified, do not fold into this PR)

- **Proactive pause-arming when any eligible parsed response reports remaining `"0"`** — deferred. It requires analyzer-derived eligibility and a single max-horizon pause candidate per response while preserving the pinned §U8.7 sinkless snapshot-derivation contract (`progressWiring.test.ts:671-690` asserts that `ghBucketedAttempt` reads zero keys from analyze-returned headers without a progress sink). Its honest benefit is suppressing NEW admissions only — in-flight requests still go out.
- Message-regex rate-limit matching: **dropped**, not deferred (see fix rationale).
- GraphQL 403 REST-style top-level `{message}` bodies and `errors[].extensions.code` are not handled as explicit classifier signals. For a 403 with remaining `"0"`, `x-github-sso` remains fatal; otherwise an exact `RATE_LIMITED`/`RATE_LIMIT` type is primary. Without either exact type, a projected `errors[].message` matching `permission|not accessible|forbidden` is fatal only when `Retry-After` is absent; all other remaining-`"0"` shapes are primary.
- runPlan (`--plan`): no requeue concept; post-fix, pre-final funded pauses sleep and retry inside `graphql()`; `ThrottleExhausted` from retry exhaustion or an unfunded cumulative-budget tail is counted as a branch-discovery error, while plan-mode owner-resolution exhaustion remains fatal. Acceptable.
- Quiet-path throttle detail (review-ratified defer): `Classification`'s primary/secondary variants drop `errors[].message` at classification time. A resulting `ThrottleExhausted` — whether from retry exhaustion or the cumulative-budget tail — carries only its generic constructor template, so requeue telemetry cannot surface the already-exceeded `errors[].message`. This is pre-existing: the `RATE_LIMITED` pat

author: jpr5
body:
The PyPI half of the v1.38.0 release failed. npm `1.38.0`, the `v1.38.0` tag and the GitHub release all went out; `publish-pytest` failed, so **PyPI is stranded on `0.5.0` while the pin says `1.38.0`**.

**Cause — the guard could never run.** The "Verify pinned npm release is published" step read the pin with `from aimock_pytest._version import AIMOCK_VERSION`. That executes `aimock_pytest/__init__.py`, which imports `_server`, which imports `requests` — and no Python deps are installed at that point in the job. Run [30947561858](https://github.com/CopilotKit/aimock/actions/runs/30947561858): `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'`. Deterministic — it would fail on **every** release, and it is the guard that exists to prove npm published before a wheel is uploaded.

**Fix.** `runpy.run_path` executes `_version.py` alone. That file is a docstring plus one assignment with no imports of its own, so the pin reads with nothing installed.

**Verified, not assumed:**
- `runpy` on the bare file → `1.38.0`, rc=0, with no package on the path.
- Control: the old form against a package whose `__init__` imports a missing module → `ModuleNotFoundError`, rc=1 — CI's exact failure reproduced.
- A missing `AIMOCK_VERSION` now raises `KeyError` rather than printing empty, so the guard still **fails closed**.
- `actionlint` clean. Workflow-only diff; no version-bearing file touched.

**After this merges**, dispatch `Release` to finish the v1.38.0 rollout: the npm publish no-ops (1.38.0 already published, the version gate skips it) and `publish-pytest` proceeds to upload `aimock-pytest 0.5.2` pinned to a version that is genuinely on npm.

author: girlbossrush
body:
Diagnoses the three `Module not found … no valid target file` errors from the wave-2 merge.

**Root cause, all three:** stale compiled trees on a freshly-pulled machine, surfaced through package-exports resolution in the docs/demo webpack graph.

- `@mailwoman/codex/es` + `/it` are new imports (`neural/placetype-pair-prior.ts`, rebuild day). The demo's curated alias list didn't cover codex, so webpack resolved them through `exports` → `out/` — and a `codex/out` predating the new subpaths fails the whole build. **Fixed here:** the barrel (exact-match) + all eight locale subpaths alias to source, matching every sibling entry in `resolve.ts`. **Proof:** built with `codex/out` deleted — exit 0, zero resolution errors (previously: exit 1, three).

author: nickgag626
body:
Tier A + B of the issue-scan plan: nine user-facing bugs and the LLM-timeout class, all in `apps/web`. Net **−175 lines**.

## Broken features fixed

| Bug | Root cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Analytics "Open PR" failed 100% of the time | Full ISO timestamp sent as `validatedOn` → apply route builds the branch name from it → `:` makes the git ref invalid | Send `YYYY-MM-DD`; apply route normalizes defensively |
| Doc generator unusable in prod | Required the removed personal-Anthropic-key flow (ignored under the proxy anyway) + 16k tokens with no timeout (guaranteed gateway 504) | Service key, 25s abort, 4096-token cap |
| Style-guide checks silently skipped for everyone (audit + PR review) | Gated on the removed personal key | Gated on the server service key — they actually run now |
| Explore opportunities could cache an empty result for an hour | Hardcoded `claude-opus-4-7`; if the proxy doesn't serve it, all calls fail, `Promise.allSettled` swallows it | Configured default model; 0/N successes throws instead of caching empty "success" |
| Feedback agent said "Add one in Settings" — field doesn't exist | Leftover of the removed key flow | Reworded to service key; removed dead `apiKey` threading + unused `AnthropicKeyPrompt` component |
| Health "Link Orphans" card opened the wrong tab | `tabValue="true-orphans"` hardcoded; no link-orphans tab existed | Added a real link-orphans tab |
| `/curl-validator` + audit cURL check errored in prod | `curl_validator.json` isn't produced by the indexer — 404 treated as an error | Hook resolves `null` (missing = normal); page explains instead of erroring |
| Batch audit with duplicate URLs: one row stuck at "pending" forever, stats double-counted | Items matched by URL via `findIndex` | Items carry a unique id |

## LLM timeout class

Same failure mode as the already-fixed deep-audit timeouts (deployment gateway kills upstream at 30s) — every remaining unbounded server-side LLM call now has an abort:

- audit route style/AI fetches → 25s `AbortSignal`
- `rules-deprecation/suggest` → 18s abort (it runs after a 10s page fetch), `max_tokens` 8192 → 4096
- chat route → 60s per-turn abort so a hung upstream can't pin the streaming invocation
- Deleted dead code carrying unbounded 16k-token calls: `applyWithAi` (never called) and the server-side `getAiSuggestions` (superseded by the client-side flow)

## Cleanup

- `getUserWithDecryptedCreds` now honors its `includeAnthropicKey` flag instead of decrypting the legacy personal key on every session load.

## Verification

Typecheck clean, 24/24 tests pass, lint shows only pre-existing warnings.

author: roseoutllc
body:
## What this fixes

The production replay still treated several fundamentally different outcomes as the same missing-pair failure. That made legitimate no-match, clarification, unsupported-market, and audited inventory-gap outcomes indistinguishable from real search defects.

## End-to-end changes

- Adds evidence-backed replay dispositions:
  - `passed`
  - `expected_constraint_no_pair`
  - `clarification_required`
  - `known_inventory_gap`
  - `unsupported_market`
  - `anchor_not_found`
  - `temporary_external_failure`
  - `fixable_regression`
- Adds explicit `blocksCanary` and `retirementEligible` ownership.
- Keeps zero results blocking unless the response provides direct evidence for a non-blocking disposition.
- Preserves raw diagnostic reasons even when a row becomes a valid non-blocking outcome.
- Adds candidate-loss stage diagnostics for:
  - profile candidates
  - geo-eligible candidates
  - domain-assigned candidates
  - taxonomy-eligible candidates
  - publishable candidates
  - final restaurant candidates
  - final activity candidates
  - rejected candidate IDs, stages, and reason counts
- Accepts generic-anchor clarification as a canonical non-blocking outcome.
- Accepts truthful named-anchor not-found outcomes without forcing legacy fallback.
- Requires an explicit inventory audit before a query can become `known_inventory_gap`.
- Keeps unexplained profile-candidate collapse, false fulfillment, omitted final pairs, legacy fallback, and temporary execution failures blocking.

## Production review integration

- Persists candidate-loss and anchor-resolution diagnostics in replay snapshots.
- Aggregates disposition frequency and counts.
- Surfaces retirement candidates separately from true failures.
- Removes non-blocking dispositions from unresolved required regressions.
- Keeps canary blocked only by real regressions, temporary failures, unresolved required blockers, or latency.

## Tests

Adds focused coverage for:

- full candidate-stage preservation
- unexplained 19-candidate collapse remaining blocking
- confirmed inventory gap becoming non-blocking only with audit evidence
- generic-anchor clarification
- named-anchor not found
- unsupported market versus supported-market defect
- required-regression cleanup
- canary behavior across expected and blocking dispositions

## Scope

This PR changes replay interpretation, evidence persistence, retirement eligibility, and launch gating. It does not weaken search constraints or silently retire zero-result searches.

author: ngc-shj
body:
## What this does

Adds a second, much cheaper eval alongside `rule-ablation/`, and reports its first result.

`rule-ablation/` asks **does this rule change a review?** — 20–35 agents and two authored fixtures per question. This asks **does this rule ever fire?** — one command, no fixtures, no agents, over the 1493 review artifacts nine sibling repos have accumulated since March.

## Why this before auditing all 74 rules

Rounds 1–9 settled the mechanism: a rule transmits the literal clauses it states, at full rate, and nothing else. That says nothing about *which* rules are worth stating clauses in. Panel-auditing all 74 the way rounds 5–6 audited five is ~300 agents plus a defect sketch per rule — worth knowing first which rules have ever produced a finding.

## Result: the catalogue is a long tail

| | |
|---|---|
| median firing rate | **0.50%** of reviews where the rule existed |
| rules firing under 1% | **48 of 74** |
| best mature rule | R2 — 5.36% (55 findings / 1026 opportunities) |

The routing protocol is being followed (RT1 cited in 628 of 1026 opportunities, R3 in 582), so these are reviewers running the check and finding nothing — not skipping it.

### Eight rules have never fired

| rule | opportunities | checked | findings |
|---|---|---|---|
| R10 Circular module dependency | 1026 | 270 | **0** |
| R8 UI pattern inconsistency | 1026 | 262 | **0** |
| R16 Dev/CI environment parity | 1026 | 247 | **0** |
| R15 Hardcoded env values in migrations | 1026 | 200 | **0** |
| RS5 | 449 | 187 | **0** |
| R33 | 977 | 166 | **0** |
| RS6 | 297 | 100 | **0** |
| R40 | 449 | 96 | **0** |

Every one of R10's 270 citations is a checklist line (`R10: N/A — flat shell sourcing, no cycles`). They cost 6.8% of `common-rules.md` and **7.5% of the digest**, which every review reads.

## Nothing is deleted in this PR

Recorded as candidates, deliberately:

1. **Prophylaxis is invisible.** Rules are read during implementation too; a rule that stops the defect being *written* shows zero findings and looks identical to a dead one. Rounds 1–3 already removed the "safety net" argument (no detection difference), but the authoring pathway was never tested.
2. **Demotion is self-fulfilling.** A rule out of the digest can never be routed to, so it can never fire, so the measurement can never be revisited. One-way door — worth walking through on purpose.

Corpus caveat: one person's repos, mostly TS/Next.js + a Swift client + shell tooling.

## Tests

Eight bats tests, each red-proved by executed mutation. **Two were rewritten mid-flight** because the first version passed against the mutation it claimed to catch:

- "a rule absent from the catalogue is not counted" — the table is driven by catalogue IDs, so it could never have shown a phantom rule regardless. Rewritten to assert against `--json`, the one output that would carry it.
- "a longer ID is not matched as a shorter one" — `\d+` is greedy, so digit truncation was never possible. Rewritten to target what the anchors actually guard: IDs embedded in longer tokens (`ERROR1`, `R1x`), red-proved against dropping each anchor separately.

That is the RT8 shape caught in our own test suite.

## Gates

- `bash hooks/check-rule-sync.sh skills/triangulate` — OK
- `bats tests/` — 1073 pass / 0 fail (1065 + 8 new)

author: chrizefan
body:
## The bug

Position-size changes rendered **`0.0% → 0.0%`**. The TRIM/ADD label was right; both weights were wrong.

The live `pm-rebalance` payload carries only `{action, ticker, rationale, target_pct}` — verified against the 2026-08-04 document, which has **no `current_pct` key at all**. `queries.ts:1180` read `Number(o.current_pct ?? 0)`, so every action started from zero.

`recommended_pct` was never broken — the mapping from `target_pct` has been there all along. I said otherwise when I filed the issue and have corrected it there.

## The part that matters: which book date

The prior weight is on the **previous** book date, not the current one. The current book already has the target applied:

| ticker | action | `target_pct` | weight on 08-04 | weight on 08-03 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| XLV | trim | 5.0 | **5.0** | **9.8616** |
| XRT | add | 10.0 | **10.0** | **4.9207** |

Reading the current book yields `5.0% → 5.0%` — no change at all, a *different* wrong answer. That was my first attempt; checking it against production is what caught it. The real moves are XLV **9.86% → 5.0%** and XRT **4.92% → 10.0%**, and `prevWeightByTicker` already existed 350 lines above for exactly this purpose.

A ticker with no prior-date weight genuinely was not held, so 0% there is real rather than fabricated — that case is an OPEN and the panel labels it so. Which is what the original `?? 0` destroyed: it made "we have no idea" indistinguishable from "it was 0%", and 0% means something specific and different.

Same defect class as #1833's fabricated `0.0%` day-change on carried prices and #1749's `today` badge over frozen content — absent rendered as a confident value.

## Why a new module

Extracted to `lib/rebalance-actions.ts` because `queries.ts` has no test harness, and this arithmetic reached users precisely because nothing exercised it.

**11 tests, fixtured on the real production payload and book weights.** That choice is load-bearing: an invented fixture that happened to include a `current_pct` key would not have caught this. Red-green verified — reverting to `?? 0` fails 4 of them.

## Verification

- **847 passed** (116 files), full olympus vitest — 11 new
- `tsc --noEmit` clean; eslint 0 errors (1 pre-existing warning in `eslint.config.mjs`)
- `make score` **10/10/10/10**

## Still open in #1850

The dedicated Actions section, the initiated-at timestamp, and the portfolio +/- indicator. Note for whoever takes them: a new-or-removed position has no rate of change, and computing a delta from 0 for a brand-new position is the same fabrication this PR removes.

Refs #1850

author: e-badillav
body:
## Summary
This PR introduces a new custom integration for Wazuh that polls the ThreatDown Nebula/OneView API for security events and injects them into the Wazuh analysis engine. The integration enables organizations using Malwarebytes Nebula to correlate endpoint detections, suspicious activity, and quarantine events with their Wazuh security monitoring.

## Key Changes
- **New integration script** (`custom-threatdown.py`): A complete OAuth2-authenticated polling integration that:
  - Fetches detections, suspicious activity events, and quarantine items from ThreatDown APIs
  - Supports both Nebula and OneView API variants
  - Implements cursor-based pagination for large result sets
  - Injects events into Wazuh via UNIX socket in the standard integration format

- **State management**: Persistent tracking of:
  - Last polling timestamp to avoid re-fetching historical data
  - Event deduplication across runs using content-based hashing and direct ID fields
  - Bounded deduplication cache (MAX_SEEN_IDS) to prevent unbounded memory growth

- **Resilience features**:
  - Execution locking to prevent concurrent runs from racing on state
  - HTTP retry logic with exponential backoff for transient failures (5xx, timeouts, connection errors)
  - Polling overlap window (POLL_OVERLAP_MINUTES) to absorb API indexing latency
  - Event size truncation to fit Wazuh's socket message limits

- **Configuration**: Environment variable support for:
  - OAuth2 credentials (CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET)
  - Account ID for Nebula variant
  - API variant selection (nebula or oneview)
  - Polling behavior (lookback hours, page size, overlap window)

- **Logging**: Comprehensive integration logging to `/var/ossec/logs/integrations.log` with event counts and error details

## Notable Implementation Details
- Event deduplication is namespaced by event type (detection/suspicious_activity/quarantine) to avoid false collisions across independent ID spaces
- Fallback deduplication uses SHA256 hashing of key fields when direct IDs are unavailable
- OneView variant has limited support (per-site polling not yet implemented for suspicious activity and quarantine)
- Designed for deployment at `/var/ossec/integrations/custom-threatdown.py` with scheduling via Wazuh's `<wodle name="command">` configuration

author: jacksonrock-personal
body:
Three changes, and one correction.

Cadence 3× daily → once, at 10:07 UTC. This is the big lever. Runs two and three searched the same window as run one against a `known` list that had just grown, and reliably found nothing; events are not announced on an eight-hour cycle. It also makes the incremental design correct rather than merely cheaper — exactly one new day enters the horizon per day, so newlyEnteredDay now lines up one-to-one with runs. The only thing 3× bought was collapsing the wait when a new metro appears, which is rare and can be handled by triggering a run by hand.

RESCAN_DAYS 2 → 1. A run covers RESCAN_DAYS + 1 near days plus the day that just entered, so this goes from four days of search surface to three.

FULL_RESCAN_MS 7 days → 3. This one can raise cost, and only in the failure case, which is when you want it to. At once a day, a missed run leaves a hole no incremental window ever goes back for — the newly entered day is offered on the day it enters and never again. Seven days meant that hole could sit most of a week.

The correction: this file, its docs and three commit messages all claimed the incremental window saved "roughly six-sevenths". It did not. At RESCAN_DAYS=2 it covered four days out of seven, about 43%. Nobody had looked at what the endpoint actually returned until the cost question was asked directly. It is now three of seven.

Also removed `const fromDays = full ? 0 : 0`, a ternary that read as if it decided something and never did.

author: kristofferremback
body:
## Problem

Where a draft lands when it is sent — which stream, and whether flat or nested — is implicit and computed per surface. The board card derives it inline; the drafts explorer derives a label from a different code path; the timeline derives nothing at all.

That is fine while every composer's stash pile is scope-exact. It stops being fine in the next chunk, where a pile is shared across surfaces: a pile that offers a draft the send would file somewhere else is a wrong-place send. An adversarial pass on the plan refuted the assumption this was built on — `planBoardReply` (`use-conversations.ts:401`) converts a **lone** channel/DM conversation into a thread off its opener, so that conversation's board reply does not land flat in the channel at all.

## Solution

> **Superseded within this stack.** This PR originally shipped `resolveDraftLandingSite` as that authority. The product owner then changed the membership model twice after testing, and the pile ended up on a different rule (`resolveDraftHomeStream` plus four explicit routes, in the PR above). Nothing ever consumed the landing-site resolver, so it and its tests were deleted here rather than left as dead surface (INV-38). What this PR still ships is the `reply-plan.ts` extraction below, which is live.
>
> The original description follows, for the record.

`resolveDraftLandingSite(scope, context)` — one authority, consulted in the same order the card uses at send time.

- `planBoardReply` first: `convertToThread` ⇒ `nested`, never flat. This is the lone-conversation case and the reason the resolver exists.
- Otherwise `boardPostLastActiveStreamId(post)` — the recency-biased stream, so a conversation that moved into a thread resolves flat in that thread, not in its anchor.
- `thread:`, `board:branch-reply:`, `board:subtopic:` ⇒ `nested` by rule; they cannot share a flat pile with anything.
- An uncached conversation ⇒ `unknown`, an explicit third state rather than a quiet `flat` (INV-11). The caller decides; the next chunk's caller fails closed.

`stream:<S>` resolves flat unconditionally rather than requiring a cached stream row — a scratchpad's `stream:draft_xxx` has no `db.streams` row, and cache-gating would make every scratchpad draft `unknown`. A not-yet-created thread never uses this scope (`stream-panel.tsx:175` gives it `thread:<anchorId>`, relocated on promotion), so `stream:<S>` always names a stream that exists or a scratchpad that will.

Supporting moves, no behaviour change:

- `planBoardReply` / `boardPostLastActiveStreamId` → `lib/board/reply-plan.ts`, so the resolver is testable without react-query and contexts. Bodies byte-identical; the param widens to a structural type.
- The board-context liveQuery → `hooks/use-board-draft-context.ts`, shared by the drafts explorer and (next chunk) the composer pile (INV-35). Its id-signature gate is preserved — it still never re-fires on a keystroke.

Nothing consumes the resolver yet. The drafts explorer renders identically: same labels, hrefs, `supportsStashRestore`, grouping and ordering.

### Deferred, needs a product ruling before the adopt chunk

The **timeline's** armed "Reply in conversation" files a lone conversation flat into the channel — it never consults `planBoardReply` — while the board card and the conversation panel both thread it. Same conversation, same first reply, two structural outcomes. Pre-existing, not introduced here, and the resolver is faithful to each scope. It is unreachable through the pile (a `nested` scope is excluded from every flat pile), but it has to be settled before the adopt chunk lets one draft move between those scopes: either the timeline armed reply consults `planBoardReply` too, or the board stops converting.

## Files

| File | Change |
| ---- | ------ |
| `apps/frontend/src/lib/drafts/landing-site.ts` | **new** — `resolveDraftLandingSite`, `DraftLandingSite` |
| `apps/frontend/src/lib/drafts/landing-site.test.ts` | **new** — one case per membership-table row, incl. both lone-conversation directions and the uncached case |
| `apps/frontend/src/lib/board/reply-plan.ts` | **new** — `planBoardReply`, `boardPostLastActiveStreamId` moved verbatim out of `use-conversations.ts` |
| `apps/frontend/src/hooks/use-board-draft-context.ts` | **new** — the id-signature-gated board-context liveQuery lifted out of `use-all-drafts.ts` |
| `apps/frontend/src/hooks/use-draft-landing-sites.ts` | **new** — hook form over the resolver; no consumer yet |
| `apps/frontend/src/hooks/use-all-drafts.ts` | Consumes the extracted context hook (+7/-103); resolution, labels and ordering untouched |
| `apps/frontend/src/hooks/use-conversations.ts` | Imports `planBoardReply` from `reply-plan.ts`; every external consumer was repointed rather than re-exported |
| `apps/frontend/src/components/timeline/message-input.tsx` | Import path |
| `apps/frontend/src/hooks/use-conversations.test.tsx` | Import path only |

## Test plan

- [x] `landing-site`, `use-all-drafts`, `pages/drafts`, `use-conversations` (vitest) — 4 files, **70 pass**
- [x] `bunx tsc --noEmit -p apps/frontend` — clean
- [x] Falsification: neutralising the `convertToThread` branch reds exactly the two lone-conversation cases
- [x] Extraction fidelity checked against `f4c359c13` token-for-token, including the empty-context early return and the dep array
- [ ] No test asserts the liveQuery re-fires the same number of times after extraction — the gate is preserved by construction (identical keys and deps), not measured

<details>
<summary>📋 Full implementation plan</summary>

https://seer.build/ws_vbyzjvdg6g/b/draft-sharing-3cd745/ — chunk 1 of 0-5. Chunk 2 makes the pile landing-site-wide; chunks 3-5 add the durable composer target, adopt-vs-move on restore, and the picker UI.

</details>

author: javierbq
body:
Cuts the macOS (Sparkle) release for **RayMol 1.9.0, build 25**.

## Why build 25

`1.8.1` was a hotfix cut off the `v1.8.0` **tag**, not master — so master's `project.yml` was never bumped past `1.8.0` / build **23**, while the live appcast serves build **24**. Sparkle compares on `CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION`, so this release needs **25** to be offered at all.

Verified that nothing from the 1.8.1 hotfix is missing on master: the only deltas are master being *ahead* (extra OBJPANEL test coverage from #241, and #229 replacing the explicit scene `runPython` calls with a centralized `cmd.scene` hook).

## What's in it

Headline is **Design mode** — on-device ProteinMPNN, macOS-only (#221 / #227 / #228). Plus per-object TTT capture in scenes (#229), the `~/.raymolrc` startup script (#226), and three fixes (#236, #237, #230). iOS-only work since v1.8.0 is deliberately excluded from the macOS notes.

Full user-facing notes: `docs/release-notes/v1.9.0.md`.

## What's New splash

Minor bump, so this adds a four-page 1.9.0 splash with **real captured hero media** (not SF Symbols): Design mode, Mutate and redesign, Scenes remember placement (looping mp4), Your own startup script. All four verified rendering in a 1.9.0 / build-25 app.

The Design mode captures had to be taken on a host Mac rather than the usual disposable VM — the VM's paravirtual GPU won't run mlx, so a VM capture would have shown an uncolored structure instead of the confidence heatmap.

⚠️ `WhatsNew.json` ships in **both** the macOS and iOS bundles and has no per-platform gating, so the two macOS-only Design pages will also render on iOS. Worded "on your Mac" as a stopgap; tracked properly in #243.

## Size note

The bundled `MPNN.mpnnpack` adds 24 MB, and being raw float tensors it compresses only 1.08× — so it adds ~22 MB to the DMG essentially uncompressed. Expect the download to go from 55.5 MB to roughly 80+ MB.

## Files

- `swiftui/project.yml` + regenerated `project.pbxproj` — version bump, new media registered
- `docs/release-notes/v1.9.0.md` — new
- `swiftui/PyMOLViewer/Resources/WhatsNew.json` + four `whatsnew-190-*` assets

author: clubanderson
body:
Two urgent fixes for the most-visible breakages on the live hive: the empty **Live Activity** rail and the empty **Ready-work queue**.

## 1. Live Activity rail perpetually empty ("Watching the hive…")
The Operations rail depended **solely** on the SSE stream `/api/contribute/events`, which returns **zero bytes** on hosted spokes — while `/api/contribute/activity` (the same source the Onboarding "Live Activity" feed uses successfully) is full.

**Fix:** on Operations-tab load, **seed + poll the rail from `/api/contribute/activity`**, narrated through the existing `ccNarrate` / `ccRenderLog`. SSE, when it works, layers live updates on top via a **shared deduped activity store** (events keyed by `timestamp+username+action+task`, so an event arriving via both poll and SSE is counted once). The `live` pill now reflects real connectivity (shows *polling* when SSE hasn't delivered). The genuine "Watching the hive…" empty state stays reachable only when the endpoint truly returns zero events.

## 2. Ready-queue empty — admission label-filter bound to the wrong field
The admission Labels filter persisted its Allow-mode tags to a field the backend never reads, so Allow + `clanker-queue` admitted **nothing** → empty queue.

**Fix:** bind Titles / Authors / Labels to the **canonical `contribute_deny_<kind>` list field in every mode**. Note on the codebase: despite the `deny` in the name, that field holds the filter's list **regardless of mode** (the mode decides allow vs deny), and it is the **only** field the backend filter (`LabelsFilterPasses` / `FilterPasses`) reads — `contribute_allow_labels` is never read by the filter (it exists only for a one-time migration). So the correct fix is to bind to the canonical field per-mode and **clear the stale `allow_labels` remnant** on save; the policy display now reads `deny_labels` in both modes too. Allow-mode + an empty list already means **"admit all"** in the backend (the footgun-safe default), so no config change was needed there. Result: Allow + `clanker-queue` admits the clanker-queue-labeled issues again.

## Tests
- Label filter binds/round-trips to the canonical field and admits the right issues (including empty-allow = admit-all).
- The rail seeds from the activity poll (not SSE-only), dedupes cross-source events, keeps the genuine empty state, and drives the live pill.
- `go build` / `go vet` / `node --check` on the extracted page script all pass.

Two follow-up PRs will carry the remaining Operations bug fixes (My-work Done filter, me-card tier-badge overlap, highlight-me row, Repos + Tier-limits Management mirror, `Fixes #2601` bot-filter) and then the additive features (Apple-Music playlist queue controls, Opportunistic Work `#2592`, file-an-issue `#2594`, hive-settings/quota `#2595`).

body:
## Проблема (P1, целевой refresh-аудит цикл 12 — см. `docs/reviews/REVIEW_LOG.md`)

`DELETE /api/users/{user_id}` безусловно удалял любого пользователя, включая:
1. Самого вызывающего администратора (self-lockout — сессия остаётся валидна до истечения 30-минутного access-токена, но повторный вход или управление системой после logout уже недоступны).
2. Последнего оставшегося администратора в системе вообще — после этого управление пользователями/камерами/настройками недоступно **никому** до перезапуска backend. `main.py:lifespan` досеивает пользователя `admin` только если такого username вообще не существует, а не по фактическому количеству администраторов — переименованный/другой-по-имени последний админ не восстановится автоматически.

RBAC-матрица ТЗ описывает роли, но не этот инвариант явно — тем не менее «администратор управляет пользователями» подразумевает, что администратор в системе всегда есть.

## Фикс

В `backend/app/routers/users.py::delete_user()`:
- Запрет удаления собственной учётной записи (`target.id == current.id` → 400).
- Запрет удаления последнего администратора по подсчёту роли (defense-in-depth: поскольку эндпоинт сам требует роль `admin`, единственный реалистичный путь к нулю админов через него — self-delete, уже перекрытый первой проверкой; второй чек фиксирует инвариант на случай будущих изменений).

## Тесты

Новый `backend/tests/test_integration_users.py` (интеграционные, реальный Postgres+Redis, как и остальные `test_integration_*`):
- self-lockout блокируется для единственного (сидового) администратора;
- проверка не срабатывает ложно, когда админов двое;
- оператор не может удалять пользователей (403);
- админ может удалять обычных (не-admin) пользователей;
- 404 на несуществующего пользователя.

Полный backend-набор прогнан локально на настоящем Postgres 16 + pgvector + Redis (venv, `pip install -r requirements.txt`): **126 passed**.

author: wuad391
body:
`app/debug_scenario` never started a scheduler — its own header says so —
but it linked one, because `Jsip_gateway.Metrics` publishes to a
`Pipe.Reader.t`.

For a script whose whole purpose is being watched by the visual
debugger, that is pure cost. Pulling the gateway also pulls
`Jsip_exchange_stats`, whose six `[@@deriving bin_io]` types each
register a writer, a reader and a type-class record at module init.
Those never die and sort first in the registry, so on the debugger's
heap pane they are **eighteen cards standing between you and the
exchange**, on every step.

## Changes

- **`Session_stats` replaces `Metrics`**, locally in the scenario: a
  `Participant.Set.t` of who traded and `float Queue.t`s of latency
  samples. Kept rather than deleted because those were the *only*
  `Core.Set` and `Core.Queue` in the whole run — dropping them would
  have cost the debugger two of the seventeen structures it knows.
- **`Protocol` moves to its own library.** 103 lines of formatting over
  `Jsip_types` and `Jsip_symbol_directory`, no Async and no RPC; it sat
  in the gateway only by habit. `Jsip_gateway.Protocol` re-exports it,
  so all fourteen users are untouched.
- **`jsip_order_book` drops `async_log`**, which nothing in it
  references.

One subtlety worth keeping: the latency samples are enqueued through a
**named local**, not `Queue.enqueue t.submit_samples`. An event rooted
at a mutation needs a named identifier, so the field form records
nothing — which is why the old `Metrics` produced only 2 `Core_queue`
events across the entire run.

## Measured on the replay dump

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Async linked | yes | **none** |
| dump | 32 MB, 1825 events | 21 MB, 1513 events |
| `Bin_prot` values | 57 | 39 (the rest are `jsip_types`' own 13) |
| live structures mid-run | 556 | 437 |
| nodes | 2782 | 1634 |
| `Core_queue` events | 2 | 65 |
| `Core_hash_queue` | 112 | 112 (the order book is intact) |

## Verified

`lib/protocol`, `lib/gateway/src`, `lib/types`, `lib/order_book/src`,
`lib/pnl`, `lib/symbol_directory`, `lib/test_harness`, `app/client`,
`app/debug_scenario`, `lib/gateway/test` and `lib/types/test` all build
clean on the standard switch. `dune runtest` hits a pre-existing
ppx_expect source-path issue when run from a git worktree — identical
on this branch and on the base commit (8 occurrences each), so it is
not from this change.

## Replaying it

From `jsip-visual-debugger`:

```sh
./cool_name.sh <this-checkout>/app/debug_scenario/bin/main.exe
```

That needs the fork's toolchain, and one local adjustment not in this
PR: the instrumented build links Core/Async v0.17, where
`Rpc.Implementations.create_exn` has no `~on_exception`. That one line
in `lib/gateway/src/exchange_server.ml` has to come out for the replay
build only — deliberately left out of this branch, since removing it
breaks the v0.18 build everyone else uses.

author: michaelphamcf
body:
[AIS-141](https://contentful.atlassian.net/browse/AIS-141)

## Summary

`getDestinationData()` had no error handling around its 6 ExO entity fetches (Design Tokens, Components, Experience Templates, Experience Fragments, Data Assemblies, Experiences). A destination space without the `exoM1` entitlement 403s on ExO endpoints (`AccessDenied: exoM1 entitlement required`), which propagated straight out of `getDestinationData()` and aborted the entire import before a single entry, asset, or content type was written — even though none of that content has anything to do with ExO. Given both CLIs default `includeExperienceOrchestration: true`, this was the out-of-the-box experience for any space without ExO enabled.

Three layers fix this:

- **Content gate** — each of the 6 ExO fetches now only fires if the source content actually contains that entity type (mirrors the existing `entries`/`assets`/`locales` pattern). An import with zero ExO entities never probes the destination at all, so there's no entitlement question to even ask for the common case.
- **Proactive entitlement check** (`spaceHasExoM1Entitlement`) — before attempting the 5 exoM1-gated types (Design Tokens, Components, Experience Templates, Experience Fragments, Experiences), checks the destination org's public entitlement set once via `GET /organizations/{orgId}/organization_entitlement_set`. This mirrors `contentful-mcp-server`'s `hasExoM1Entitlement` helper (AIS-191), adapted to check the one org we already know instead of every org the token can see. A confirmed-missing entitlement short-circuits with **one** clear message instead of 5 separate per-type 403s. `dataAssemblies` is deliberately excluded — confirmed live it isn't actually gated by `exoM1` the same way as the other 5 — so it always goes through its own independent fetch-and-catch. If the check itself can't complete (network error, space lookup failure), it fails open to the existing reactive per-type catch rather than treating "inconclusive" as "not entitled."
- **Severity split** in the reactive catch (`cursorPaginatedQueryOrWarn`) — the confirmed "ExO not enabled" case still warns and continues, so it doesn't affect overall run success (the common, expected case once gated on real source content). Any other error on these fetches (bad token, a real outage, etc.) now logs as an `error`, so the overall import correctly reports failure instead of silently succeeding despite dropped ExO content.

## Live verification

Ran the built CLI against two real spaces — one confirmed to lack `exoM1`, one confirmed to have it (checked directly against the entitlement endpoint, not inferred):

| Scenario | Destination | Result |
|---|---|---|
| No ExO content in source | lacks `exoM1` | Exit 0, zero ExO probes at all |
| ExO content (incl. Data Assemblies) | lacks `exoM1` | One combined error for the 5 gated types; Data Assemblies still fetched independently and succeeded; exit 1 |
| ExO content in source | has `exoM1` | Normal fetch, no entitlement error, exit 0 |
| ExO content in source, one type forced to a genuine (real, unmocked) 500 | has `exoM1` | Correctly classified as non-entitlement, logged as an error, did not abort the run |
| No ExO content in source | has `exoM1` | Exit 0, zero ExO probes — proves the content gate wins regardless of destination capability |

## Test plan
- [x] `test/unit/tasks/get-destination-data-exo.test.ts` (18 tests) and new `test/unit/utils/publish-exo-entities.test.ts` (7 tests for `spaceHasExoM1Entitlement`) — cover the content gate, the proactive-check composition (definitively missing / present / inconclusive), the severity split, and that `dataAssemblies` always fetches independently.
- [x] Full unit suite passing, no regressions. `tsc --noEmit` clean. Lint diff-clean against this file's pre-existing baseline.
- [x] Live-verified all 5 scenarios above against real spaces (table above).

author: pyup-bot
body:
This PR updates [Django](https://pypi.org/project/Django) from **4.1** to **6.0.8**.



<details>
  <summary>Changelog</summary>
  
  
   ### 6.0.8
   ```
   ==========================

*August 4, 2026*

Django 6.0.8 fixes one security issue with severity "high", two security issues
with severity "moderate", one security issue with severity "low", and several
bugs in 6.0.7.

CVE-2026-15307: Server-side file-write and request forgery via spatial lookups
==============================================================================

Spatial lookups allowed ``str`` and ``dict`` lookup values to be passed to
:class:`~django.contrib.gis.gdal.GDALRaster` when they represented rasters.
Depending on the raster driver, this could write a file to disk (in some cases
enabling remote code execution) or issue a network request as the Django
process user. Because the admin changelist permits filtering via
:meth:`~django.contrib.admin.ModelAdmin.lookup_allowed`, the flaw was reachable
by staff users with view permission on any registered model containing a
spatial field.

The following types are now disallowed by spatial lookups:

- ``dict``
- A ``str`` that is not a valid
  :class:`~django.contrib.gis.geos.GEOSGeometry`, e.g. a serialized dictionary

This is a backward incompatible change. As a reminder, all untrusted user input
should be validated before use. For that reason, assignments to model fields
are unaffected and still accept these input types.

For guidance on how to keep using these types in spatial lookups, on validating
untrusted input, and on further security considerations, see
:ref:`raster security considerations <raster-security>`.

This issue has severity "high" according to the :ref:`Django security policy
<severity-levels>`.

CVE-2026-15337: Potential denial-of-service vulnerability in ``check_for_language()``
=====================================================================================

:func:`~django.utils.translation.check_for_language` was subject to a potential
denial-of-service attack when checking many distinct, very long language codes.
Each code was used as a key in an in-memory cache, consuming process memory.

The ``language`` value reaches this function through the
:func:`django.views.i18n.set_language` view (not active by default) from POST
data. Since request data is limited by :setting:`DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE`
and the cache is configured to store a maximum number of entries, the memory
that could be consumed was bounded.

To mitigate this vulnerability, language codes longer than 500 characters are
now rejected before the cached lookup.

This issue has severity "low" according to the :ref:`Django security policy
<severity-levels>`.

CVE-2026-15830: Potential denial-of-service vulnerability via nested geometry collections
=========================================================================================

:class:`~django.contrib.gis.geos.GEOSGeometry` was subject to a potential
denial-of-service attack when provided deeply nested ``GEOMETRYCOLLECTION``
objects, leading to a segmentation fault in GEOS. A maximum depth of 198
``GEOMETRYCOLLECTION``\s is now enforced for the well-known text (WKT) format,
and a maximum number of 198 ``GEOMETRYCOLLECTION``\s in total (breadth and
depth) is enforced for well-known binary (WKB).

:ref:`Lookups against spatial fields <spatial-lookups-intro>` and the
:class:`~django.contrib.gis.forms.GeometryField` form field were also affected.

The limit can be customized through the new ``max_geom_collections`` argument,
available on :class:`~django.contrib.gis.geos.GEOSGeometry`, the
:attr:`form field <django.contrib.gis.forms.Field.max_geom_collections>`,
and the :attr:`model field
<django.contrib.gis.db.models.GeometryField.max_geom_collections>`. The limit
is not applied to GeoJSON inputs, as they were parsed by GDAL and are not
affected.

This issue has severity "moderate" according to the :ref:`Django security
policy <severity-levels>`.

CVE-2026-15920: Potential cross-site scripting via ``URLField`` values in the admin
===================================================================================

The admin renders :class:`~django.db.models.URLField` values as clickable links
on changelist views and read-only fields. The link was generated without
validating the value as a safe URL, so a stored value using a potentially
dangerous scheme was rendered as a link.

``URLField`` values shown via ``display_for_field`` are now validated using
:class:`~django.core.validators.URLValidator` before a link is rendered, and
displayed as plain text if validation is failed.

This issue has severity "moderate" according to the :ref:`Django security
policy <severity-levels>`.

Bugfixes
========

* Fixed a regression in Django 6.0 that caused
  :meth:`~django.db.models.query.QuerySet.bulk_create` to crash on databases
  that support returning rows from bulk inserts when a related object providing
  the primary key was saved after assignment (:ticket:`37234`).

* Added compatibility for ``sqlparse`` 0.5.5 (:ticket:`37235`).


==========================
   ```
   
  
  
   ### 6.0.7
   ```
   ==========================

*July 7, 2026*

Django 6.0.7 fixes three security issues with severity "low" and one bug in
6.0.6.

CVE-2026-48588: Potential exposure of private data via cached ``Set-Cookie`` response
=====================================================================================

:class:`~django.middleware.cache.UpdateCacheMiddleware` and
:func:`~django.views.decorators.cache.cache_page` avoided caching responses
that set a cookie while varying on ``Cookie`` only when the incoming request
contained no cookies at all. When the request already carried an unrelated
cookie (such as a language or theme preference cookie), the protection did not
apply, allowing a response that sets a session or other sensitive cookie to be
stored in Django's shared cache.

This issue has severity "low" according to the :ref:`Django security policy
<severity-levels>`.

CVE-2026-53877: Heap buffer over-read in ``GDALRaster``
=======================================================

When :class:`~django.contrib.gis.gdal.GDALRaster` was instantiated with a bytes
object representing a raster file, the
:attr:`~django.contrib.gis.gdal.GDALRaster.vsi_buffer` property could over-read
the allocated buffer by approximately 32 bytes. This could result in
information disclosure of adjacent heap memory or, in rare cases, a
segmentation fault. Only rasters stored in GDAL's virtual filesystem were
affected.

This issue has severity "low" according to the :ref:`Django security policy
<severity-levels>`.

CVE-2026-53878: Header injection possibility since ``DomainNameValidator`` accepted newlines in input
=====================================================================================================

:class:`~django.core.validators.DomainNameValidator` accepted newlines in
domain names. If such values were included in HTTP responses, header injection
attacks were possible. Django itself wasn't vulnerable because
:class:`~django.http.HttpResponse` prohibits newlines in HTTP headers.

The vulnerability only affected uses of ``DomainNameValidator`` outside Django
form fields, as ``CharField`` strips newlines by default.

This issue has severity "low" according to the :ref:`Django security policy
<severity-levels>`.

Bugfixes
========

* Fixed a regression in Django 6.0 where the PBKDF2 and MD5 password hashers
  raised :exc:`UnicodeDecodeError` for :class:`bytes` passwords that were not
  valid UTF-8. Passwords supplied as :class:`str` or as UTF-8 :class:`bytes`
  are unaffected (:ticket:`37184`).
